items.title: Athenian democracy excluded most of the population
items.claim: How inclusive was 5th-century BCE Athenian democracy?

options.text: Citizen-men over 18 (perhaps 30,000-40,000) voted in the assembly (ekklesia); women, slaves (perhaps 80,000-100,000) and metics (resident foreigners, perhaps 25,000) had no political rights — citizens were probably 10-20% of the city's population
Women had equal political rights with men

items.reveal:
The Athenian assembly met around 40 times a year on the Pnyx hill. Decisions on war, treaties and major legislation required a quorum of around 6,000. The Council of 500 (boule), juries and most magistracies were filled by lot — a feature of radical democracy.

Pericles' citizenship law (451 BCE) restricted citizenship to those with two Athenian parents. Aristotle's 'Athenaion Politeia' (4th century BCE) describes the system. Thucydides records Pericles' Funeral Oration extolling Athenian democracy in 431 BCE.

Women, even citizen-women, had no vote. Slaves performed much of the manual labour that supported leisure for political participation.
items.why: Calling Athens 'the cradle of democracy' is true with major qualifications. Its political innovations were real and influential — but its exclusions were severe enough that modern democracies share aspirations more than they share institutions with it.

items.title: Constantine legalised Christianity in 313 CE but converted slowly
items.claim: When did the Roman Empire become Christian?

options.text: Constantine made Christianity the state religion in 312

The Edict of Milan (313) granted religious toleration; Constantine increasingly favoured Christianity but was baptised only on his deathbed in 337; Theodosius I made Christianity the state religion by the Edict of Thessalonica in 380
The empire remained pagan until 600 CE

items.reveal:
Constantine's victory at the Milvian Bridge (28 October 312) over Maxentius came after a reported vision of the Chi-Rho symbol with 'in hoc signo vinces' (in this sign you will conquer). The Edict of Milan, agreed with Licinius in 313, granted religious toleration to all.

Constantine convened the Council of Nicaea (325) and built churches across the empire. He moved the capital to Constantinople (founded 330). He was baptised on his deathbed in 337 by an Arian bishop, Eusebius of Nicomedia.

The Edict of Thessalonica (380) under Theodosius I made Nicene Christianity the state religion. Pagan worship was progressively restricted; the Olympic Games were banned in 393.
items.why: Religious change at imperial scale is a process, not a moment. The 67 years between Milan and Thessalonica saw a tolerant empire become a Christian one — a transformation studied by every subsequent religious-political shift.

items.title: Anglo-Saxon law replaced revenge with a price list

options.text: A trial by combat for serious crimes
A 'man-price' — compensation paid to a victim's family or to a victim of injury, set by social rank (a king's wergild far higher than a ceorl's) to end blood feuds
A property tax owed to the lord

items.reveal:
Aethelberht's law code (Kent, c. 600 CE) — the earliest surviving English legal text — sets compensation for injuries with itemised precision: four shillings for an outer ear, twelve for the inner. Murder of a freeman (ceorl) was 200 shillings; a thegn 600; a king's son much higher.

Wergild aimed to substitute payment for cyclical feud. It coexisted with the death penalty for some offences (theft, treason). The Norman Conquest gradually replaced wergild with crown justice — crimes against the king's peace rather than against persons.
items.why: 'Justice' has had many shapes. Anglo-Saxon law was rational, written and surprisingly modern in seeing crime as economic harm — but built around social hierarchy in a way modern law explicitly rejects.
